title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the lack of effective vaccines or antiviral therapies for Marburg virus (MARV), a deadly zoonotic illness. The research sought to design novel multi-epitope self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine candidates targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the design and in-silico cloning of two saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) into the standard saRNA model, incorporating validated epitopes and suitable adjuvants. The study did not involve human or animal participants.
analysis.methods: The study utilized immunoinformatics approaches to identify and validate epitopes, conjugate them to adjuvants, and incorporate them into the saRNA model. Biophysical analyses were conducted to assess the stability and solubility of the vaccines. Immune simulations were performed to evaluate the potential immune response.
analysis.main_results: The study demonstrated significant affinity of the designed vaccines to TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, and TLR7, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by molecular dynamics simulations. The vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immune responses, evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production, and remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as novel and promising, indicating the potential for the designed vaccines to elicit strong immune responses. The study highlighted the use of immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology in the design of saRNA vaccines against MARV.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of effective vaccines against MARV, contributing to the prevention and control of Marburg virus disease. The study's approach may also be applicable to other filoviruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies to establish the safety and efficacy of the vaccine candidates conclusively. The evidence strength is moderate due to the in-silico nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccines against Marburg virus using immunoinformatics. The vaccines showed significant affinity to TLRs and triggered robust immune responses in immune simulations. Further in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish their safety and efficacy.

title: Filovirus Seroreactivity Beyond Virus-Specific Outbreak Regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 2015-2023

analysis.research_question_and_background: Using a multiplexed multi-filovirus immunoassay, we assessed antibody reactivity against antigens of filoviruses linked to human disease, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus (MARV), and Sudan virus (SUDV), among eleven cohorts from seven provinces between 2015-2023 (n=5,852).
analysis.study_design_and_population: Participants with median fluorescence intensity values exceeding established antigen-specific cutoffs were classified as seroreactive.
analysis.methods: Seroreactivity estimates varied by cohort site, with 60.8% of participants (n=175/288) in Mongala Province in April 2016 considered seroreactive against BDBV GP.
analysis.main_results: In adjusted analyses, site was the primary predictor of seroreactivity, with odds for BDBV seroreactivity 9.1-fold (95%CI 7.0-11.9) and 9.5-fold (95%CI 6.9-13.2) higher in Mongala and Tshuapa provinces than in Kwilu.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Seroreactivity against glycoprotein (GP) targets of all four viruses were detected in every cohort, demonstrating evidence of filovirus or an antigenically related exposure well beyond known outbreak regions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may reflect zoonotic spillover events, leading to undetected human-to-human filovirus circulation, including paucisymptomatic or asymptomatic infections, or exposure to as-yet unidentified antigenically cross-reactive viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Overall, these results indicate widespread, geographically heterogeneous filovirus seroreactivity across sampled cohorts.

analysis.summary_en: Using a multiplexed multi-filovirus immunoassay, we assessed antibody reactivity against antigens of filoviruses linked to human disease, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus (MARV), and Sudan virus (SUDV), among eleven cohorts from seven provinces between 2015-2023 (n=5,852). Participants with median fluorescence intensity values exceeding established antigen-specific cutoffs were classified as seroreactive. Seroreactivity estimates varied by cohort site, with 60.8% of participants (n=175/288) in Mongala Province in April 2016 considered seroreactive against BDBV GP. In adjusted analyses, site was the primary predictor of seroreactivity, with odds for BDBV seroreactivity 9.1-fold (95%CI 7.0-11.9) and 9.5-fold (95%CI 6.9-13.2) higher in Mongala and Tshuapa provinces than in Kwilu. Seroreactivity against glycoprotein (GP) targets of all four viruses were detected in every cohort, demonstrating evidence of filovirus or an antigenically related exposure well beyond known outbreak regions. These findings may reflect zoonotic spillover events, leading to undetected human-to-human filovirus circulation, including paucisymptomatic or asymptomatic infections, or exposure to as-yet unidentified antigenically cross-reactive viruses. Overall, these results indicate widespread, geographically heterogeneous filovirus seroreactivity across sampled cohorts.
